title: Russia Says Fuel Crisis Is Easing as Refineries Restart
summary: Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the domestic fuel shortage is easing as several refineries resume operations. While supply at filling stations and deliveries to agricultural producers have improved, some regions, notably parts of Siberia, remain tense. The shortages followed months of Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries and export infrastructure, prompting a diesel export ban and disruptions at Black Sea terminals that have also affected Kazakhstan's output.
content:
The fuel crisis in Russia has started to ease in recent days as some refineries have restarted operations, Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said.

"The situation is gradually stabilizing, a number of oil refineries became operational again. The balance is better now, and the situation at fuel filling stations has considerably improved, including when it comes to supplying agricultural producers," Interfax quoted the official as saying.

"The situation remains quite tense in some regions, especially in some regions in Siberia. We are effectively resolving issues of fuel supply manually at the federal headquarters with regions and companies," Novak added, calling the crisis "temporary."

Russia has been suffering from gasoline and diesel shortages for more than two months amid peak demand season after Ukraine's drone campaign struck multiple Russian refineries and forced many large processing sites offline in the spring and early summer. Early this month, Russia banned diesel exports to protect domestic supply, a move that has tightened an already constrained global diesel market.

Since the spring, Ukraine has expanded efforts to disrupt Russian fuel logistics by targeting supply routes, vessels and refineries. In recent weeks Kyiv's forces focused attacks on Russia-linked vessels in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, with Ukraine reporting more than a hundred vessels hit by drones. Several Russian oil export terminals on the Black Sea have also gone offline following these strikes.

Russia's largest Black Sea oil export terminal, the Sheskharis terminal at Novorossiysk, effectively went offline recently, days after drone attacks had shut the neighboring Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) terminal. The suspension of CPC terminal loadings prompted Kazakhstan to cut oil production, with output at Chevron's giant Tengiz field reportedly falling by more than half as storage filled and producers were forced to reduce pipeline flows.

Russian officials say they are coordinating supply solutions at the federal level with regional authorities and companies, but analysts warn that liability of further attacks, export restrictions and chokepoints in the Black Sea corridor continue to pose risks to both domestic supplies and global oil and diesel markets.

By Charles Kennedy for OilPrice.com
